description: Reference grades for the Grader-agreement eval (target: ≥85% of Grader scores within ±1 of these). Scale 0–5 as in apps/server/src/agents/prompts/grader.md. Facts are drawn from source.md.
labelledBy: Claude (draft, 20 Oct 2026). Pending review by Paul: adjust any score you disagree with; your judgement is the reference.

questions.question: What is the Merkle root and where is it stored?
facts: The Merkle root is the single hash left after recursively hashing pairs of transaction hashes.
It summarises all the transactions in the block.
It is stored in the block header.

questions.question: How is a Merkle tree built from a block's transactions?
facts: Each transaction is hashed to form a leaf.
Consecutive pairs of hashes are concatenated and hashed to form the parent.
This repeats level by level until one hash, the root, remains.
If a level has an odd number of hashes, the last hash is duplicated.

questions.question: Why does changing one transaction change the Merkle root?
facts: Changing a transaction changes its hash.
That changes every parent hash on the way up.
So the root changes, and the header no longer matches.

questions.question: How can a lightweight client check that a transaction is in a block without downloading every transaction?
facts: The client keeps block headers, which contain the Merkle root.
A full node sends a Merkle path: the sibling hashes from the transaction up to the root.
The client hashes up the path and compares the result with the Merkle root in the header.

questions.question: How big is a Merkle path, and why does that matter?
facts: A Merkle path needs about log2(N) hashes for N transactions.
It grows very slowly as blocks get bigger, so proofs stay small (a few hundred bytes) even for thousands of transactions.

questions.question: What links one block to the previous block?
facts: Each block header contains the hash of the previous block's header.
This forms a chain back to the genesis block.
